====================================================================================================

Is super a bigger political bomb than Medicare? We're about to find out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
03:07:57 UTC
12:07:57 KST

analysis
Jim Chalmers says the next election is a 'referendum' on super. Is the outcome clear?
Barnaby Joyce had just said "lie" for the 17th time when the line went dead.
A few moments later, dialled back into his Radio National interview, he joked listeners had missed him in "full flight" about Jim Chalmers's claim One Nation and the Coalition were "against universal super". It was, he said, a lie to rival the infamous "Mediscare".
It's a telling comparison. Joyce fought the 2016 election when Bill Shorten's Labor ran the brutally effective scare campaign that the Coalition planned to privatise Medicare.
And Chalmers, invigorated by comments about super from Pauline Hanson and Liberal Andrew Bragg, has wasted no time in framing the next election as a super "referendum", spamming social media with claims his opponents want to "destroy" the system.
That's a bit much. Hanson only said super should be "lightened up a bit", perhaps by letting people access more of their funds pre-retirement. Bragg was more colourful, calling compulsory super "a loss of liberty", but his colleagues ran a mile from him.
Still, the line isn't totally fanciful either. One Nation has flagged more policies to come, and there is genuine hostility to super among Coalition MPs, several of whom told the ABC this week they did want to carve out a point of difference with Labor on the subject.
Some within Labor are salivating at that prospect. Asked whether super was as much of a vote-winner as Medicare, a senior Labor figure jubilantly declared: "It's bigger."
But on the right, some believe that voters weighed down by economic gloom will be tempted by the thought that super is their money and they should access it now, not later. So would a super referendum deliver the resounding Yes vote Labor expects?
Supercharged retirement
Since it began in 1992, compulsory super has substantially boosted the wealth with which Australians retire. That's even before the system is "fully mature" — that is, when retirees have had super for their whole working lives, a milestone still years away.
Super's logic is neat: require people to save some money for their own retirement, give everybody access to the power of compound returns on long-term investments, and reduce the need for pension payments. Labor hails it as "the envy of the world".
But the fact remains that putting money away for tomorrow means less money today. In a legal sense, the amount employers must pay into their workers' super — currently 12 per cent of their wages — is on top of their wages, not instead of them.
But for businesses, the dollar is still a dollar, and a 2020 Grattan Institute report based on a study of enterprise agreements found super increases had come at the expense of wage increases most of the time.
This is contentious terrain, and that finding landed in the middle of a political debate about whether the compulsory amount should increase from 9.5 per cent to 12 per cent. The Coalition resisted, but Labor delivered it in government.
Labor politicians strenuously resist the idea that workers must choose between more super and more wages. But a hint at what they really think is that they have no plans to move to a 15 per cent guarantee, Paul Keating's original vision.
Comparing the pair
At the same time, Treasury and Grattan have warned in recent years that super may be over-preparing people for retirement, such that retirees spend very little of their super before they die or even increase their wealth, passing on large inheritances.
A Treasury retirement income review in 2021 studied the accounts managed by one large super fund and found that members died with 90 per cent of the super they had retired with on average.
Ironically, Labor itself has used this argument when it has proposed less generous tax treatment for those with very high super balances — and the Coalition has usually been on the opposite side of that debate.
But when it comes to the super guarantee, the roles are reversed, and the Treasury finding of 2021 informed a view among many on the conservative side that the guarantee was too high.
Some would even like to wind back the clock, lowering the guarantee to perhaps 10 per cent. Several Liberal politicians told the ABC this had been discussed internally but was viewed as a risky proposition and had slim prospects of becoming opposition policy.
That would truly make the election a referendum on super. The idea could have political appeal if it was presented to voters as a wage rise. But there would be no guarantee that businesses would pass the savings on and, if they did, it would be an inflation risk.
Instead, the Coalition has gone to the last two elections campaigning to erode super a different way; by letting first homebuyers tap their super for a home deposit, an idea spearheaded by Bragg and now-shadow treasurer Tim Wilson.
It's not clear this has been a major factor in either election, for good or ill, but it is hated by economists who say it will push up house prices and will not solve the crisis.
That may even be a design feature. Liberals claim those who drain their super would be no worse off because their money would make a similar return once invested in their home. But that's only true if house prices keep growing above inflation forever.
When do we want it? Now
The Coalition's plans for that policy are ambiguous. But Hanson is now swimming in the same waters. Her policy, which does not exist yet beyond some vague statements, is to allow people to draw down on their super as a cost-of-living measure.
Here, unlike the super housing policy, the money withdrawn would likely be spent, not invested. An academic study of the Morrison government's pandemic policy to let some people access $20,000 of their super found gambling was a major spending category.
The line of "gambling with your future" almost writes itself, and One Nation would open itself to a fierce campaign from Labor and a well-endowed super industry which has spent decades building public support for super as the bedrock of financial security.
A war of slogans would follow: "It's your money" up against "It's your future".
Loading
Indicators of future performance
For either One Nation or the Coalition to win that campaign, it would likely need to find some way to discredit those high reserves of public affinity for super. Bragg has been trying this in his own way for years with his claims of "corruption", with little success.
But a sleeper issue on the government's agenda could change this: an overhaul of the "performance test", the rules governing how super funds can invest members' money, a dry and technical process led by assistant treasurer Daniel Mulino.
The industry says the current benchmarks are too restrictive, forcing them into safe bets and inhibiting them from investing in start-ups or innovation. Funds are so constrained that they have effectively run out of Australian investments and are hunting abroad.
Labor has signalled it will broaden the criteria without compromising the requirement for funds to make responsible investments and solid returns. But it is also planning to set "national priorities", such as investment in housing and renewables.
That is a red rag to a bull for conservative super sceptics, and the Coalition has been watching warily for some time. But this week, it was Hanson who blew it up.
"Jim Chalmers cannot stop spending, and now he has his eyes on Australians' superannuation to fund more of Labor's bad ideas," she said in a social media post this week. "Your super is not Labor's piggy bank … Jim Chalmers should keep his hands off."
There is no more truth in the idea that the super performance test changes are a Labor raid on superannuants than there is to Chalmers's claims about his opponents "destroying" super — fighting liar with liar, to use Joyce's word. But it's a reminder that a super war could damage both sides.
Former treasurer Wayne Swan, who now heads a large super fund, acknowledged the risks but said it was a fight Labor was right to pick and should be confident of winning.
"The thing is, it's a cheap trick, a mirage," he told the ABC. "You're telling people you're giving them something when you're just taking it away."

Screened Space is the headquarters and experience centre of an electrical switches company, located within the densely packed historic core of Vijayawada in Andhra Pradesh. It is conceived as an architectural response to its complex urban condition where streets are narrow, services are exposed and buildings line tightly with little to no space between them. Within this setting, the project establishes a distinct presence by negotiating visibility, climate control and privacy.

Warning for travellers as hotspot for Australian tourists brings in new tax

IN BRIEF
- Fiji tourism operators with a turnover above $1.3 million will be taxed 5 per cent from 1 September.
- Australian and Fiji travel associations say they weren't consulted about the change and costs may be passed on to travellers with existing bookings.
The Fijian government will introduce a new tourism services tax for large-scale tourism operators next month, with travel industry experts warning that the costs could be passed on to customers.
The 5 per cent tax will apply from 1 September. The change has been criticised by travel associations in Fiji, Australia and New Zealand, who claim they were not properly consulted.
The Australian Travel Industry Association (ATIA) said the measure could catch out travellers who have already booked trips to Fiji from September onward, as travel agents and operators face confusion over how to administer the tax.
"The design and roll out reflect a complete lack of understanding of how the travel booking ecosystem works, and it is travellers and travel businesses who will pay the price for that failure," ATIA CEO Dean Long said.
"Travellers are the ones left exposed. Families with September school holiday bookings already paid in full, and travellers on large group, corporate and film production bookings, are being asked to find extra money for a holiday they thought was settled months ago. That is not how you treat people who chose Fiji in good faith."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The change forms part of wider taxation amendments enacted as part of Fiji's 2026-2027 national budget, passed last month.
It will affect tourism operators — including hotel, tourism and cruise businesses — with an annual turnover above FJ$2 million (approximately $1.3 million).
According to Fijian finance minister Esrom Immanuel, revenue from the tax will be used to support Fiji Airways.
"The revenue generated will be ring-fenced and fully directed to Fiji Airways, which continues to face financial pressure from rising aviation fuel costs and its ongoing recovery from losses incurred during the COVID-19 pandemic," Immanuel told local media in June.
It's reported that the tourism tax will generate around FJ$70 million ($44.7 million) for the airline. The Fijian government is the largest shareholder of Fiji Airways.
Consultation with Fijian government
ATIA confirmed it will meet with the Fijian government to discuss the tourism services tax, which it said arrived with "zero consultation".
Long said there is ongoing confusion over how the tax is collected, saying that members of the travel industry in Australia and New Zealand — which represent Fiji's largest tourism markets — were not consulted on the change.
"None of this needed to happen. The tax arrived with zero consultation with the travel industry in Australia or New Zealand despite the significant importance of these markets to Fiji," he said.
ATIA said there are still questions about how net rates (base prices which exclude discounts, commissions or fees) will be taxed, while the distinction between suppliers and agents remains "unresolved".
The Travel Agents' Association of New Zealand (TAANZ) said it was concerned with the way the tax is being implemented, and proposed that existing bookings be grandfathered.
"Grandfathering existing bookings is the fairest outcome. It protects travellers who purchased in good faith, gives the travel industry certainty and allows the new tax to be implemented cleanly for new bookings from 1 September," TAANZ CEO Julie White said.
SBS News has contacted the Fijian government's Ministry of Tourism for comment.
According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, Fiji was one of the top 10 short-term return destinations for Australian travellers in June 2026.
Almost 37,000 Australians returned from short stays (less than one year) in Fiji in June this year. That's compared to around 35,000 visitors in June 2025.
In a statement issued in June, the Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association (FHTA) said the tourism industry did not propose, endorse or "broadly agree" to the tax.
FHTA CEO Fantasha Lockington added that retroactively adding costs would "undermine confidence in Fiji's tourism product".
"Operators cannot simply return to guests, agents or wholesalers to recover another 5 per cent without risking disputes, cancellations, destination and brand reputational damage or margin loss," she said, adding that industry operators do not agree to absorb the tax.
"Indications from members suggest the majority, if not all, will pass it on in its entirety," she said.
Lockington noted that Fiji Airways remains vital to the country's connectivity, visitor arrivals, trade and employment. However, she believes the carrier should be funded through a "national fiscal response", not a tax imposed on the travel sector.
In July, Immanuel told Fijian broadcaster FBC News he was "surprised" by FHTA's statement and claimed the proposal had received support during discussions before the budget.

- The dispute over the islands has stalled a World War II peace treaty between Russia and Japan, with limited dialogue since former PM Shinzo Abe's negotiations.
AI generated
MOSCOW – Russia conducted a rare missile exercise involving naval vessels and a land-based launcher near islands in its Far East that are also claimed by Japan, adding to recent friction between the two nations.
Missiles were launched from a nuclear-powered submarine, a guided-missile cruiser and the Bastion coastal defence system around the Southern Kuril islands, the Russian Pacific Fleet said on Aug 20, without providing the date of the exercise, according to the Interfax news agency.
The missiles were fired at targets more than 300km away and hit them, according to the report.
The Pacific Fleet didn’t provide a precise location for the exercise, but Russia deployed Bastion coastal defence batteries on Iturup Island, known in Japan as Etorofu, in 2016.
In response to the exercise, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi told reporters: “Russia’s military buildup on the four Northern Islands runs counter to Japan’s position and is unacceptable,” according to Kyodo News.
The southern Kuril islands are controlled by Russia after the Soviet Union seized them from Japan in the final days of World War II.
Russian President Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the territory last week when he travelled to Iturup, prompting a protest from Tokyo.
Putin’s visit and the missile test come as Japan has aligned with western nations in support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian invasion, including the imposition of sanctions on Moscow.
Tokyo has also supplied non-lethal support for Ukraine’s military, including body armour and transport vehicles.
During his visit to the Far East, Putin said that Japan had recently changed its attitude toward Russia without provocation.
He criticised sanctions and said Russia had been described as a major threat in Japanese defence documents.
The dispute over the islands has prevented Moscow and Tokyo from signing a formal World War II peace treaty.
While Russia’s possession of the Kurils is “enshrined in international documents,” Moscow was still prepared to seek a solution through a peace treaty with Japan, Putin said last week.
Former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe sought to reach an agreement with Putin under which two of the islands would be returned to Japan, but since then there’s been little prospect of renewed dialogue.
Unlike her immediate predecessors, current Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has yet to hold talks Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, prompting some speculation that she might try to restart negotiations over the disputed islands with Russia. BLOOMBERG

Storms and possible tornadoes pummel the Northeast US, flooding roads and damaging beaches
NEW YORK (AP) — Heavy rain and winds pounded the Northeast U.S. on Thursday as storms tore through a beach on Long Island, stranded dozens of people in their cars in New Jersey and knocked out power in parts of Delaware’s capital city.
Photos and video shared on social media show debris thrown in the air and pummeling rain as a possible tornado touched down at Atlantic Beach on Long Island’s outer barrier. It tore apart a major beach club, leaving broken beach chairs and wood beams littered across the shoreline.
Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman said there were no reports of serious injuries or deaths, but there had been damage to property and a search team was making sure no one was trapped in the cabanas. He declared a state of emergency.
“There are reports of people trapped in their vehicles due to flooding in the south shore, and first responders are assisting in their rescue,” he said in a statement.
The Sun and Surf Beach Club said buildings had been significantly damaged and it temporarily closed that club and nearby Silver Point.
The National Weather Service had warned of waterspouts, tornado-like hazards that happen over water, in the area but wasn’t able to immediately confirm a tornado on the beach.
Bryan Ramsey, a meteorologist for the weather service in New York, said the storm was moving East offshore Thursday evening and was expected to taper over the next several hours.
In other parts of New York, flooding caused part of the Long Island Expressway in Queens to close in both directions, according to New York City Emergency Management. Photos on social media showed lines of stopped cars as emergency crews traversed the water.
In Jersey City, New Jersey, emergency crews rescued 69 people trapped in cars that had been overtaken by flash flooding Thursday, said Mayor James Solomon. Emergency crews waded through roads with knee-high water with small inflatable boats to help those stranded.
A likely tornado touched down in Dover, Delaware, and caused significant damage across the city, the police department reported. There were no reports of serious injuries, police said.
“Dover — please take this seriously. Stay home. Stay safe,” the department said on Facebook.
Photos and video online show fallen trees, downed power lines and flooded roads.
The Delaware Electric Cooperative said more than 1,000 customers didn’t have power in the northern part of its service area, but within a few hours most of the outages had been fixed.

The crash happened near Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, approximately 450 miles (725 km) west of Anchorage, Alaska.
“This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve,” U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, said in a statement.

Davis described those on board as “dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment. Our absolute priority right now is providing unwavering support to their families, friends and teammates during this devastating time. We are profoundly grateful for the swift and tireless response of our search and recovery professionals.”
Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, said earlier Thursday evening that two pilots and six passengers were on board.

- The E1 project threatens the contiguity of a future Palestinian state and has drawn warnings about breaching international law, with Britain planning sanctions against those involved.
- Israel defended its actions, rejecting criticism and accusing Britain of ignoring Palestinian extremism, while Peace Now highlighted the timing before Israeli elections as politically motivated.
AI generated
PARIS - France, Italy, Britain and Germany on Aug 20 piled on mounting international condemnation of a major settlement project in the occupied West Bank, after Israeli authorities opened bidding for more than 1,200 homes in the area.
The E1 plan was green-lit by Israel in 2025 and would further separate east Jerusalem, occupied and annexed by Israel and predominantly inhabited by Palestinians, from the West Bank.
“At a time of grave instability in the West Bank with unprecedented levels of violence by settlers against civilians, and serious restrictions on the Palestinian economy, this decision is even more concerning,” the joint statement from Paris, Rome, Berlin and London said.
“We urge the Government of Israel to retract these plans immediately and end its expansion of settlements in the West Bank,” it added, warning businesses against bidding for the construction tenders at risk of “involving themselves in serious breaches of international law”.
The UN secretary-general has said the E1 plan posed an “existential threat” to a contiguous Palestinian state.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot called the tenders “unacceptable” on Aug 20, saying the project “would seriously undermine the viability of the two-state solution”.
His condemnation echoed a statement by Britain’s top diplomat Ed Miliband on Aug 19 demanding an end to the project and settlement expansion in the West Bank, with London summoning Israel’s charge d’affaires.
‘Israel will defend its rights’
Miliband said he delivered the message directly to his Israeli counterpart Gideon Saar.
Saar on Aug 20 said he rejected “outright” Miliband’s statement and “the patronising tone of his words”.
“The Jewish people have the right to live throughout the Land of Israel, just as the British have the right to live in London and throughout the United Kingdom,” he wrote on X.
Saar went on to accuse Britain of “blaming only Israel while ignoring Palestinian extremism” which he said was fuelling anti-Semitic attacks against the British Jewish community.
“The UK Government’s decision to damage the relationship between our countries is deeply unfortunate,” he added, vowing that “Israel will defend its rights, its interests and its people”.
The British government on Aug 19 also pledged to unveil “a comprehensive set of measures” in the coming weeks, including sanctions targeting people involved in the “illegal settlement expansion”.
Israel approved the plans for the roughly 12sq km parcel of land known as E1 just east of Jerusalem, in August 2025.
The plan seeks to build around 3,400 homes on the ultra-sensitive tract of land, which lies between Jerusalem and the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim.
The latest tender covers more than 1,200 housing units, according to Israeli NGO Peace Now.
Peace Now said Israel’s housing ministry published the tender on Aug 18 and immediately opened it for bids.
Submissions are due by Oct 19, one week before Israeli elections scheduled for Oct 27.
The group said the homes accounted for about one-third of the planned E1 development and accused the government of trying to advance construction commitments before the vote.
Israel heavily restricts the movement of West Bank Palestinians, who must obtain permits from authorities to travel through checkpoints to cross into east Jerusalem or Israel.
In 2025, Britain and France were among 21 countries who condemned Israeli approval of the E1 project, calling it a violation of international law and urging Israel to reverse the decision.
Excluding east Jerusalem, the West Bank is home to around three million Palestinians. About 500,000 Israeli settlers also live there.
Violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers has increased since the unprecedented Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas from the Gaza Strip. AFP

Hong Kong convicts Tiananmen vigil leaders
August 21, 2026
A Hong Kong court on Thursday convicted two pro-democracy Tiananmen activists under Beijing's controversial national security law for "incitement to subversion."
Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, had organized candlelight vigils to mark Beijing's deadly 1989 Tiananmen crackdown. They were charged in 2021 and both pleaded not guilty.
They face a maximum prison term of 10 years and are expected to be sentenced at a later date.
Germany, France and Taiwan call for immediate release of activists
Germany and France on Friday morning published a joint statement to say that both "deeply regret the guilty verdict against human rights lawyer and democracy activist Chow Hang-tung."
The statement called for the immediate release of Chow and added that "peaceful advocacy for human rights does not constitute a crime."
Chow was the recipient of Franco-German Human Rights Award in 2023.
Taiwan also called on China to "stop political persecution."
Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council, which oversees the island's China policy, expressed "deep regret and sorrow" and called on the Chinese Communist Party and Hong Kong government to "immediately release those detained in this case."
What else do we know about charges against the pro-democracy activists?
Hong Kong judicial officials claimed the pair "incited other persons to organize, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power."
Prosecutors had argued they "endanger(ed) national security in the name of human rights."
Public commemorations of the deadly Tiananmen crackdown, when Beijing sent troops and tanks to crush protests calling for political reform in and around the capital's Tiananmen Square, have been effectively banned since the 2020 imposition of the national security law on Hong Kong.
The controversial law came after Hong Kong's massive anti-government, pro-democracy protests in 2019.

Liberia receives first group of "third country" deportees from U.S., officials say
Unknown

Liberia receives first group of "third country" deportees from U.S., officials say
The West African nation of Liberia received the first group of "third country" deportees from the U.S. on Thursday, including migrants from Latin America, U.S. officials told CBS News.
Roughly 20 deportees from different countries landed in Liberia, after being deported from the U.S.
A U.S. official, however, told CBS News that after the plane carrying the deportees arrived in Liberia, a small group of them resisted and refused to deplane.
They were escorted off the plane, but then returned to it, the official said. Their whereabouts are unknown.
Liberia is the latest country to accept deportees who are not its citizens as part of President Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration and an aggressive White House effort to deport migrants to so-called third countries where they have no ties.
The government of Liberia has said it intends to accept up to 1,200 third country deportees from the U.S. over the next year, and that the new arrivals will be allowed to apply for asylum there.
Liberia is also where the Trump administration has said it is trying to deport Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the man who was wrongfully deported to El Salvador last year and then returned to the U.S. to be prosecuted on human smuggling charges. That effort has been blocked for now by a federal judge in Maryland.
The Trump administration has brokered third country deportation agreements with dozens of nations across the globe, including African countries plagued by armed conflict, political tumult and human rights abuses, including South Sudan, the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
U.S. immigration officials have also sent regular deportation flights to Ghana, Equatorial Guinea and other African countries that have agreed to receive deportees from other nations.
Human rights activists have denounced the third country deportations as inhumane and illegal under international law, saying some countries are returning deportees to places they fled because of persecution.
But the Trump administration has defended the legality and merits of the deportations, portraying them as an effective way to deter illegal immigration.
For the most part, the administration's third country deportation effort has focused on migrants whose home countries limit or reject U.S. deportations or who've won legal protections from being sent back to their homelands.

United Kingdom

Bali jails Swiss tourist for insulting sacred Day of Silence
- Published
A Swiss tourist has been sentenced to one year in prison for insulting a sacred religious event on Indonesia's holiday island of Bali.
In a now-removed video, Luzian Andrin Zgraggen, 26, had filmed himself walking to an empty beach during the Hindu holiday of Nyepi, describing the scene as "crazy".
He was arrested in March after the video sparked widespread anger among Balinese on social media.
Nyepi, also known as the Day of Silence, is an annual holiday during which the usually bustling tourist island goes quiet, as people stay home and refrain from making loud noises. The restrictions apply to everyone on the island regardless of religion, including tourists.
On Nyepi, the island's airport shuts down and internet access is cut.
Entertainment events are restricted and even the use of electricity is discouraged.
Residents typically stock up on groceries ahead of Nyepi so they can stay at home during the holiday.
On Nyepi, which fell on 19 March this year, Zgraggen filmed himself breaking the ban on going out, in an Instagram post captioned with expletives, local media reported.
"What the defendant did offended the Balinese people, hurt their faith and provoked public outrage," the presiding judge said, according to the Associated Press.
Zgraggen said during his trial that he did not understand the extent of Nyepi restrictions and did not mean to insult the Balinese.
"I deeply regret what I did, I apologise to the Balinese people," the Associated Press reported him as saying in court.
Tourists have previously been detained or deported for violating Nyepi restrictions.
Bali has seen tourist numbers recover past its pandemic lull. Last year it welcomed a record seven million international visitors.
But along with the surge in tourism comes misbehaviour that has vexed locals and Balinese authorities. Foreigners have been penalised for offensive acts at religious sites, forming exclusive tourist enclaves and flouting traffic laws.
Authorities have vowed to tighten scrutiny of the island's tourists and crackdown on unruly foreigners.

Hong Kong: ‘Dismaying’ Tiananmen convictions part of campaign to erase Chinese history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
02:28:51 UTC
11:28:51 KST

Responding to the convictions of activists who organized Tiananmen vigils in Hong Kong, Amnesty International Hong Kong Overseas spokesperson Fernando Cheung said:
“This dismaying verdict underlines how Hong Kong’s National Security Law is being used to punish people for peacefully remembering one of the darkest chapters in recent Chinese history.
“For decades, Hong Kong was the only place on Chinese soil where large-scale public remembrance of the Tiananmen crackdown could take place. Today’s decision marks another grim milestone in the government’s deliberate campaign to erase that legacy and silence those who seek truth, justice and accountability.
Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks said:
“Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan have not committed any recognizable crime; they have been convicted solely for their role in organizing peaceful commemorations of the people killed by the Chinese authorities on 4 June 1989.
“The Hong Kong authorities should quash these convictions and end the ongoing persecution of people seeking to keep the memory of Tiananmen alive.
“Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan are prisoners of conscience who should never have been prosecuted in the first place. They must be released immediately and unconditionally.”
Background
Hong Kong’s High Court today convicted Tiananmen activists Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan of “inciting subversion of state power” under the city’s National Security Law. Chow and Lee, along with Albert Ho Chun-yan, who previously pleaded guilty to the same charge, will be sentenced at a later date and face up to 10 years’ imprisonment.
Chow and Lee were among seven members of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (Hong Kong Alliance) charged with different offences under the Beijing-imposed law in September 2021. Both have been held in pre-trial detention ever since, having been repeatedly denied bail. They have been designated prisoners of conscience by Amnesty International.
Amnesty International has repeatedly raised concerns that the National Security Law, enacted in June 2020, is being used to target civil society groups, journalists, political activists and academics for actions that are fully protected under international human rights law.
The Tiananmen vigils commemorated the events of 4 June 1989, when Chinese troops opened fire on students and workers who had been peacefully protesting for political reforms in and around Beijing’s Tiananmen Square. Hundreds – possibly thousands – of people were killed. Tens of thousands more were arrested across China in the suppression that followed.
In the 37 years since the crackdown, all discussion of the incident has been heavily censored in China, and authorities have effectively erased it from their version of history.
From the beginning, commemorating the Tiananmen crackdown was forbidden in mainland China. But in Hong Kong, crowds reaching hundreds of thousands of people would gather annually in centrally located Victoria Park to peacefully remember those killed. The vigil participants regularly called on the Chinese authorities to reveal the truth about what happened and accept accountability for the atrocity; for thirty years, local government did not, in practice, interfere or object.
The last major vigil organized by the Hong Kong Alliance was held in 2019. The Hong Kong vigil was banned in 2020 and 2021, ostensibly on COVID-19 grounds. Since then, the National Security Law has effectively criminalized peaceful protest in the city – including Tiananmen commemorations.

Hong Kong Tiananmen vigil organiser, former leaders guilty of inciting subversion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
02:28:28 UTC
11:28:28 KST

Hong Kong Tiananmen vigil organiser, former leaders guilty of inciting subversion
Court rules alliance’s push to end ‘one-party dictatorship’ violated national security law, as city leader John Lee says it showed hatred of Beijing
The now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil and two of its former leaders have been found guilty of inciting subversion under the national security law by advocating an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.
In a 216-page judgment delivered at West Kowloon Court on Friday, three High Court judges ruled that any attempt to overthrow or undermine the Communist Party of China’s leadership could constitute a subversion offence because the country’s constitution does not permit Western-style democracy.
They found the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung had incited public hatred towards the party by likening Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in 1989 to local authorities’ suppression of the 2019 anti-government protests.
While stressing it was not unlawful for the alliance to organise vigils to mark the crackdown, the panel said the defendants had used the annual event to attract new supporters and instigate them to take action to oust the ruling party.
The group had drummed up public support through the operation of the June 4 museum, publication of periodicals and messages posted on its website, the court ruled.
“The evidence of this case showed that even after the implementation of the national security law, [the defendants] still continued to advocate and spread the goal of ‘end one-party dictatorship’ … thereby stirring up the hostility of their target audience towards the [party] as well as eroding and undermining the public’s confidence in its leadership,” the judges said.

After GERD, can Egypt shape Ethiopia’s next Nile dams?
The projects mark a new test for Egypt after it failed to prevent construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
Egypt’s response to Ethiopia’s new Nile dam plans is centred on diplomacy, international pressure and cooperation with Sudan, rather than trying to stop construction outright. However, the experience of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) has exposed the limits of Cairo’s influence.
The revival of three proposed Blue Nile hydropower projects – Karadobi, Mandaya and Beko Abo – will test whether Egypt can turn more than a decade of opposition into practical leverage over how Ethiopia develops the river.
The projects have been discussed for years. A 2024 academic study drawing on Nile Basin Initiative-sponsored work listed all three among proposed Blue Nile projects and noted that Karadobi and Beko Abo were considered alternatives in one potential three-dam configuration.
What is new is Ethiopia’s reported move to advance them. In March, the country’s Water and Energy Ministry announced plans for the projects, according to subsequent reporting. Their combined generating potential has been reported at about 5,700 megawatts, although the figures and specifications could change because the projects remain at the planning stage.
The announcement came months after Ethiopia inaugurated the GERD in September 2025, despite years of objections from Egypt.
Why does Ethiopia want more dams?
For Ethiopia, developing the Blue Nile is closely tied to electricity generation, economic growth and energy security. Addis Ababa argues that expanding hydropower is essential for a country where millions of people have historically lacked reliable access to electricity.
The three projects fit into that wider strategy. However, their eventual impact on Egypt and Sudan will depend on what Ethiopia builds and how the facilities are operated.
Ezekiel Gebissa, an Ethiopian professor at Kettering University in the United States, told Al Jazeera that the consequences would depend on the scale and purpose of the projects. “Smaller dams could generate electricity for local communities without significantly reducing the volume of water reaching downstream countries,” he said, while projects linked to large-scale irrigation could have greater implications for Egypt and Sudan.
The impact will depend on various factors, including reservoir size, filling schedules, water releases and operating rules. A dam designed mainly for electricity generation would have different consequences from one linked to large-scale irrigation.
For now, the projects represent a potential new source of tension rather than proof that they will reduce the water reaching Egypt.
Why is Egypt concerned?
For Egypt, the Nile is the country’s main source of freshwater. Any major change upstream is viewed through the lens of national security.
Cairo’s concern is not Ethiopia generating electricity. It is what happens when water is stored and managed upstream, particularly during periods of drought. Egypt has therefore pushed for rules covering dam operations, drought management, water releases and information sharing.
Last September, Egypt again raised the issue at the United Nations Security Council, arguing that Ethiopia’s inauguration and operation of the GERD violated its international obligations and called for a binding agreement. Those were Egypt’s stated legal and political positions, not findings by the council.
The dispute reflects two different priorities. Ethiopia views the Blue Nile as a resource for development, while Egypt seeks guarantees over the water flows on which it depends.
What did the GERD change?
The GERD demonstrated both the reach and the limits of Egypt’s diplomatic strategy.
Ethiopia inaugurated the dam on September 9, 2025, after years of negotiations with Egypt and Sudan failed to produce the binding agreement Cairo wanted. The nearly $5bn project, funded largely by Ethiopia itself, has an installed generating capacity of about 5,150 megawatts and is now a major part of Ethiopia’s electricity system.
For Egypt, the lesson was clear: diplomatic pressure could raise international attention but could not prevent Ethiopia from completing the project.
The focus has therefore shifted. Instead of trying to stop a single dam, Cairo is now seeking a role in how existing and future projects are designed, filled and operated.
Sudan’s role
Sudan remains central to Egypt’s approach because it lies between Ethiopia and Egypt and is directly affected by developments on the Blue Nile.
However, Khartoum is not simply aligned with Cairo.
Sudan could benefit from more predictable river flows and Ethiopian electricity, while also seeking greater transparency, information sharing and safeguards around upstream projects.
Mekki Elmograbi, a Sudanese governance expert, said transparency from Ethiopia was the starting point for cooperation. “Ethiopia must share more information with Sudan and Egypt; transparency is the first step toward cooperation,” he told Al Jazeera. “Who knows whether the new projects are good or bad for Sudan if there is not enough information?”
Elmograbi said Sudan should seek cooperation with both Ethiopia and Egypt to ensure major projects do not harm its interests. But Sudan’s ability to play a larger diplomatic role is constrained by its ongoing war.
While Sudan shares some concerns with Egypt, it also has its own relationship with Ethiopia and its own priorities, including access to electricity and effective management of the river.
What leverage does Egypt have?
Egypt’s strategy has centred on diplomacy, international pressure and cooperation with Sudan, aimed at pushing Ethiopia towards greater transparency and negotiated rules.
The experience of the GERD shows that Cairo’s strongest tools are political and diplomatic rather than coercive. Egypt can raise international attention, seek support from regional partners and push for agreements on issues such as data sharing, drought management and dam operations.
The challenge is that these tools are unlikely to give Egypt the ability to stop Ethiopia from pursuing new hydropower projects or to control decisions made in Addis Ababa.
Horn of Africa analyst, Abdiwahab Sheikh, told Al Jazeera that Egypt has “meaningful but limited leverage” over Ethiopia. He said Cairo’s strongest tools are diplomacy, alliances, international law and coordination with Sudan, while economic pressure is weaker and military coercion carries significant risks.
The three Blue Nile projects will test whether Egypt can convert diplomatic pressure into practical influence. For Sheikh, the path forward lies in negotiated rules rather than confrontation.
“A practical arrangement is possible if Ethiopia, Egypt and Sudan accept transparent information exchange, advance notification, adaptive dam-management rules and mechanisms for addressing droughts and downstream impacts.”

BERLIN, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Cologne has secured the long-term future of forward Said El Mala, extending the highly rated teenager's contract until 2031 and handing him the club's iconic No. 10 shirt.
The Bundesliga club announced the agreement Thursday, ending speculation over the 19-year-old's future after his breakthrough season attracted interest from elsewhere.
El Mala emerged as Cologne's leading scorer last season, finding the net 13 times in his first Bundesliga campaign while establishing himself as one of the team's most important attacking players.
The forward said conversations with coach Rene Wagner and managing director Thomas Kessler convinced him that Cologne remained the right environment for his continued development.
"Since I arrived, the club has given me a good feeling every day," El Mala said. "I feel enormous trust and great appreciation here. That is why I am staying."
El Mala will wear Cologne's No. 10 shirt, a number that had not been assigned to a player in a competitive match since Germany international Lukas Podolski left the club in 2012.
Kessler said El Mala's performances had naturally attracted attention from other clubs but that discussions with the player and his family had reinforced the belief that Cologne was the best place for his next stage of development.
"We came to the conclusion together that his potential is far from exhausted and that he has very good conditions here to take the next steps in his development," Kessler said.
El Mala joined Cologne from third-tier side Viktoria Cologne alongside his brother Malek in the summer of 2024, with both players returning to Viktoria on loan for the 2024-25 season.
After an impressive campaign in the German third division, El Mala earned selection for Germany's squad at the 2025 European Under-19 Championship, scoring four goals as the team reached the semifinals.
He then stepped into Cologne's first-team squad and enjoyed an outstanding debut season in the Bundesliga, making 34 league appearances, scoring 13 goals and adding five assists. He also played twice in the German Cup.
His performances earned him a place with Germany's under-21 team and his first call-up to the senior national side.
Kessler praised El Mala's attitude during preseason and said Cologne expects the teenager to remain a central figure in the club's plans. ■

Kovac: Dortmund must improve, Bayern must slip to close title gap

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:08:39 CST
11:08:39 KST

DORTMUND, Germany, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Borussia Dortmund coach Niko Kovac has played down expectations of a Bundesliga title challenge, saying his side must make significant progress while Bayern Munich would also need to fall below its usual standards for the gap between the two clubs to close.
Kovac made his comments at an international media roundtable in Dortmund on Thursday, two days before Dortmund hosts Bayern in the Franz Beckenbauer Supercup at Signal Iduna Park. The match will be the first competitive fixture of the new season for both teams and an early indication of whether Dortmund can move closer to Germany's dominant club.
Bayern enters the match as Bundesliga and German Cup winner, while Dortmund qualified after finishing second in the league last season.
The two teams were the closest rivals for much of the 2025-26 campaign, with Dortmund making a strong recovery after Kovac took charge during the previous season. At one stage, Dortmund reduced Bayern's lead to three points, but the defending champion eventually pulled away to secure the title on Matchday 30.
Bayern finished the season with 89 points, 16 more than Dortmund's 73, and won both Bundesliga meetings between the sides. Bayern earned a 2-1 victory in Munich in October before a 3-2 win in Dortmund in March extended its advantage to 11 points and effectively ended Dortmund's title hopes.
Asked whether Dortmund could mount a stronger challenge this season, Kovac remained realistic.
"Bayern Munich is always the favorite," he said. "We are here to challenge, but last season we were 16 points behind them. 16 is a big gap."
"To close this gap, a lot has to happen. We have to play over our capacities, and Bayern also have to play under their capacity."
The Croatian coach said Dortmund would focus on performances rather than making ambitious predictions.
"I'm a guy who is first working and then speaking," Kovac said. "I don't like to speak first and then to work."
Kovac said the team's level would become clearer after the opening five or six Bundesliga matches, but insisted Dortmund would give everything in pursuit of its goals.
The coach is encouraged by Dortmund's summer rebuild, which saw several experienced players depart while younger talents were brought into the squad.
"We are mixing a good team," Kovac said. "We kept the spine, the experienced players, and now we are trying to create the BVB from the past a little bit, with young talents who are willing to compete."
Kovac emphasized that Dortmund's success will depend on finding the right balance between youth and experience. Younger players can challenge established teammates, while senior figures can demonstrate the standards required to succeed at the highest level.
"The mixture is important," he said. "The experienced players can show the young players what is necessary to become a top player, to become a top professional."
Kovac has built his coaching philosophy around adapting to the players available rather than following a fixed style. Reflecting on his impact since taking over at Dortmund, he said improving fitness, mentality and tactical understanding had all been important.
Asked to define "Niko Kovac football," he rejected the idea that it was simply based on discipline and physical intensity.
"First of all, it's successful football," he said.
"As a coach, you need to see what kind of players you have, what kind of situation you have, and you must always adapt. If you always play the same and you're never adapting, I think you can't be successful." ■

Interview: Chinese modernization offers insights for development paths, says senior Tajik official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:08:38 CST
11:08:38 KST

DUSHANBE, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese modernization, a senior Tajik politician has argued, has charted a path distinct from the Western model -- one that offers valuable experience for developing countries seeking a route to modernization suited to their own conditions.
Under the leadership of the Communist Party of China (CPC), China has made remarkable achievements in socioeconomic development, improved people's living standards and strengthened its global influence, Maliksho Nematzoda, first deputy chairman of the ruling People's Democratic Party of Tajikistan, told Xinhua in an interview.
Nematzoda noted that especially since the 18th National Congress of the CPC, China has comprehensively deepened reform, further advanced the fight against corruption, accelerated the transformation of government functions, carried out strategic economic restructuring, and actively implemented the innovation-driven development strategy.
In his view, these measures have laid a solid foundation for the sustained and sound development of the Chinese economy, promoted greater social harmony and stability, and continuously improved people's living standards.
"China's experience lies in its commitment to sustainable development, giving priority to infrastructure development, actively expanding mutually beneficial international cooperation, and other aspects," Nematzoda said.
The Tajik politician noted that China has been committed to a people-centered development philosophy, paying particular attention to improving people's well-being and enhancing their sense of fulfillment with the achievements of development.
He said that this approach has become an important foundation for China's long-term social stability and the sustained improvement of people's living standards, and also provides valuable experience for other countries advancing their modernization.
According to Nematzoda, Chinese modernization is not a ready-made model that can simply be transplanted to other countries.
"It represents a system of governance principles and practical experience that can be applied flexibly in light of the characteristics of each country. Every country should, on the basis of its own history, culture and national conditions, independently explore a development path suited to its own realities, while maintaining independence and at the same time actively integrating into the global economy," he said.
Nematzoda also expressed hope for further strengthening coordination between Tajikistan and China within the framework of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the China-Central Asia mechanism, as well as deepening exchanges and mutual learning between the ruling parties of the two countries.
He voiced confidence that the development of inter-party exchanges will help strengthen political mutual trust, deepen exchanges of governance experience, inject new impetus into the common development of the two countries, and further consolidate the comprehensive strategic partnership between Tajikistan and China. ■

TAIEX rises on low trading volume Thursday

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s stock index ended higher Thursday, but trading activity remained subdued with trading volume below recent levels.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index, or TAIEX, briefly climbed above 45,000 points during the session before coming under selling pressure. Late gains in TSMC helped lift the index, which closed up 214.39 points, or 0.48%, at 44,933.74, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Turnover totaled NT$793 billion (US$24.9 billion). The total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$146.89 trillion, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
Among the most heavily weighted stocks, TSMC rose 1.06% to close at NT$2,375. Foxconn gained 0.61% to NT$246.5, while ASE rose 0.34% to NT$590. MediaTek fell 3.77% to NT$3,700, and Delta Electronics declined 1.13% to NT$1,745.
Memory stocks recovered after a pull-back in the previous session. PSMC, Winbond Electronics, and Nanya Technology rose 1.05%, 5.06%, and 7.48%, respectively, on heavy turnover, according to Sinotrade.
Macronix International, Phison Electronics, Apacer Technology, AP Memory Technology, Formosa Advanced Technologies, and Team Group also advanced. With major global memory chipmakers Micron Technology and SK Hynix shifting production capacity toward more advanced products, Taiwanese memory makers are expected to see stronger demand for traditional memory in the second half of the year as supply continues to tighten.
Gallium arsenide (GaAs) and optical communications stocks also advanced. IntelliEpi hit the daily limit-up, while Pcl Technologies rose 5.14% and LandMark Optoelectronics gained 4.82%.
Demand for optical communications equipment and components is increasing as AI applications require higher transmission capacity. GaAs, a compound semiconductor, is well suited to AI data centers because it supports high-speed, low-latency communications and reliable performance under heavy workloads, according to CMoney.
Container shipping stocks also remained strong with the third-quarter peak shipping season underway. Wan Hai Lines gained 4.32%, Evergreen Marine rose 3.87%, and Yang Ming Marine Transport advanced 2.89%.
Consumer battery module stocks came under pressure as the recovery in consumer electronics demand remained uneven. Dynapack International Technology, Simplo Technology, and Celxpert Energy all fell.
Passive component stocks retreated after strong gains in the previous session. Industry leader Yageo lost 2.43%, while Prosperity Dielectrics, Nichidenbo, and Walsin Technology also moved lower.
Senior analyst Chien Po-yi (簡伯儀) said the TAIEX remained under pressure near recent highs but found buying support. Relatively low turnover suggested that the correction had not been accompanied by a significant increase in selling, making a major move in either direction less likely in the short term, according to CTEE.
Trading volume will be key to the market’s next move, Chien said. A rebound accompanied by higher turnover could send the TAIEX back toward its previous high, while a decline on heavy trading could lead to further losses.
Chien added that recent investor interest in shipping, automation components, and electronic materials suggests that fundamentals in some non-AI industries are gradually improving. If the broader market avoids major volatility, sector rotation and individual stock performance could continue to shape market movements. Chien advised investors to focus on industries with relatively low valuations and signs of gradual improvement in their fundamentals.

====================================================================================================

All the winners of coveted CBCA award gold stickers in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
02:01:13 UTC
11:01:13 KST

All the winners from the 2026 Children's Book Council of Australia Book of the Year Awards
Growing up in Bendigo, Zeno Sworder spent a lot of time outdoors.
"My dad wasn't a big fan of technology, so we had no car, no television, no screens in the house," he tells ABC Arts.
"I spent all my time wandering outside … I would climb all the trees in my neighbourhood."
At the top of his street, there was one tree that stood out from the rest, with branches that were the perfect height for a kid to climb.
"I spent a lot of time up in that tree, and I would often talk to it," Sworder recalls.
These childhood memories partly inspired Sworder's latest picture book, Once I Was a Giant, about a tree that is cut down and turned into a pencil.
It's a book that he says "honour[s] the relationship that people can have with different forms of life".
Once I Was a Giant is one of the winners at the 2026 Children's Book Council of Australia (CBCA) Awards, taking home the prize for Picture Book of the Year.
The judges described the book — which also won the Victorian Premier's Literary Award for children's literature and Book of the Year and Children's Picture Book of the Year at the Australian Book Industry Awards — as "a wonderful mixture of the sophisticated and complex".
Other CBCA award winners include Darkest Night, Brightest Star by Barry Jonsberg, named Book of the Year for Older Readers; Inked, written by Karen Wasson and illustrated by Jake A Minton, which won Book of the Year for Younger Readers; and The Emperor's Egg by Rae Tan, which took out Early Childhood Book of the Year.
This year marks the 80th CBCA Awards, which were established in 1946. Past winners of the coveted CBCA award sticker include Markus Zuzak, Melina Marchetta and Shaun Tan.
Sworder says the win — his second CBCA Award for Picture Book of the Year, following My Strange Shrinking Parents in 2023 — is a "huge honour".
"[It's] very special because I was one of those kids who would wander into the library without knowing much about what the good books were," he says.
"Those little stickers were a sign or a guiding post that this may be worth your time … To now be able to put one of those stickers on my book is hugely meaningful."
'Like writing a poem'
On the cover of Once I Was a Giant is an illustration of a tiny, caped figure — the wanderer — embracing an enormous tree in a forest.
However, the story begins with a series of images of a "picture-book maker" with writer's block who lives in "a concrete box" in the city.
"It's a story about a pencil that's recounting its life as a tree that grew up in a vast forest and the relationship that it formed with a small wanderer who passed through that forest every year," Sworder, who lives in Melbourne with his family, explains.
The pencil comes into the possession of the artist, through whose hand the story unfolds.
As Sworder was working on the book, protests to end logging in native forests were happening in Victoria.
The episode prompted Sworder and his daughters, now aged nine and 14, to begin reading books about the natural world.
Together, they learned about the social lives of trees: how they were connected by their root systems and fungal networks, sharing nutrients and even warning each other of danger.
Sworder began to wonder: If a tree was sentient, what kind of personality would it have?
Inspired, he set out to write a story that explored ideas of interconnection and metamorphosis and the divide between the urban and natural worlds.
Sworder likens writing a picture book, which is generally less than 500 words in length, to writing poetry.
"[A picture book has] to be very direct, yet still try to carry not only a story but some emotion," he says.
"Like a poem, you're aiming to create a larger space within a very small number of words and to try to connect it to the reader's life in some way to fill in those emotional moments and create a little bit more impact and drama."
The illustrations add extra layers of meaning.
"Because I write and illustrate, I'm able to hold things back from the words and present them in the illustrations instead," Sworder explains.
"I love playing with the way the two forms are able to bounce off each other with the illustrations telling more of the emotional story and the text telling more of the conscious story and what's going on in the plot."
A lucky break
As a teenager, Sworder dreamt of being a comic book artist but ended up becoming an immigration lawyer in between working a variety of other jobs.
"I bounced around a lot," he says.
"I've worked in many Chinese restaurants; I taught English. But whatever job I was doing to get paid, I've always written stories or drawn in my spare time. That was just the way that I processed the world."
When his father and his grandmother, who was Chinese, died when his wife was pregnant with their youngest daughter, he decided to take what he'd learned from them growing up and turn it into a picture book.
"I sent it out to a hundred different agents and publishers," Sworder says. "I had a spreadsheet and got absolutely no response back."
His luck changed when he sent it to a local publisher, Thames and Hudson.
"They were willing to take it on," Sworder says.
"The advice I'd received from some of the other agents was that it's a good book but because the main character was very culturally specific, the market appeal of the book would be limited.
"When I spoke to Thames and Hudson, I asked them if it would be an issue and they said that the energy of the little girl and her personality was what made them want to take that book on in the first place, and so they stuck to it, which I'm incredibly grateful for."
The result was This Small Blue Dot, which was named a Notable Book for Younger Readers at the 2021 CBCA awards and won Sworder the prize for Best New Illustrator.
Exploring contemporary masculinity
Darwin author Barry Jonsberg says Darkest Night, Brightest Star — winner of the older readers category — is a departure from his usually humorous books.
The novel's narrator, 13-year-old Morgan Pickford, lives with his father and older brother, Mitch, after their mother left when Morgan was two.
"He's brought up in a household that is dominated by toxic masculinity," Jonsberg, who was an English teacher for 38 years, says.
Morgan's father places great value in athletic prowess and pushes the unwilling Morgan to play sport.
"He wants his son to become a star," Jonsberg says.
Reluctantly, Morgan chooses soccer to please his father, who Jonsberg says "puts him through very rigorous training exercises so that he can be the very best that he can be".
It's only through friendship outside his family unit — with a boy at school called Gray and an elderly woman with dementia — that he learns being a man doesn't mean following his father's toxic example.
The judges praised Darkest Night, Brightest Star for the way it tackled contemporary issues around masculinity.
"This unvarnished and harshly realistic look at a boy discovering the toxicity and dysfunction of the world he inhabits is heartbreaking, but hopeful," they said in their report.
The seed for the book came from a story Jonsberg's wife, also an English teacher, told him after work one day about a conversation she had with a year 10 student.
"[He] said, 'I've always tried to please my father, but I don't think I ever will,'" Jonsberg recalls.
"The student didn't say any more, and my wife didn't push it because it didn't seem appropriate to her at the time, and we discussed the whole idea of parental expectations and how that can be damaging if parents push a kid in directions the kid doesn't want to go."
Jonsberg began writing Darkest Night, Brightest Star the following day.
"It's a story about Morgan's development as a person and finding the things that he loves to do," he says.
"It's also about compassion, kindness and understanding."
Fighting the fall in reading rates
Sworder says the CBCA plays a crucial role in the children's literature landscape.
"It's so valuable to have a body there to take the work seriously, to celebrate it, and then to encourage students throughout Australia to read and enjoy books."
Both Sworder and Jonsberg want to see more young people reading.
"It's a depressing scenario — all the evidence seems to suggest that, particularly for young adult readers, reading rates are declining not just in Australia but across the world," Jonsberg says.
"I worry about the future generations. If people stop reading, then I think that's nothing short of a tragedy."
Jonsberg — the author of more than 20 books, including 2013's My Life as an Alphabet, adapted into the 2019 film H Is for Happiness — is doing what he can to encourage kids to read.
"In my own small way, I'm trying to write entertaining and relevant books that hopefully will get some young readers thinking: 'Hey, books aren't such a bad thing, and maybe I'll give it a go,'" he says.

Two-thirds of Ukrainians believe future will bring positive changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Two-thirds of Ukrainians believe future will bring positive changes
That is according to a survey conducted by Gradus ahead of Ukraine's 35th Independence Day, Ukrinform reports.
Ukrainians see victory as more than just the end of the war. They also see it as an opportunity to strengthen the state, develop businesses, modernize infrastructure and expand international cooperation.
In the fifth year of the full-scale war, more than 90% of respondents describe contemporary Ukrainian society as troubled, unstable and difficult. At the same time, nearly half of those surveyed see it as active, diverse, interesting and progressive.
Despite the difficulties of the present, two-thirds of Ukrainians surveyed believe that things will change for the better. Significantly, this belief does not mean an absence of fear or doubt. When thinking about their own future, respondents feel both hope (47%) and anxiety (43%). Other key emotions include optimism, confusion and fear. A similar picture emerges when respondents consider the future of Ukraine.
The survey was conducted through self-administered questionnaires among Ukrainian citizens aged 18-60. The sample consisted of 1,000 respondents.

Nancy Kissinger, wife of former US Secretary of State, dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21

10:59:00 KST

Nancy Kissinger, wife of former US Secretary of State, dies at 92
Robert D. McFadden
- Nancy Kissinger, wife of former US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, died at 92, known for her political savvy and support during his diplomatic missions.
- She was part of a high-profile couple, active in Washington and New York social scenes, and stood by her husband through his controversial political career.
- Nancy Kissinger's life included notable incidents, such as defending her husband in court and testifying in a high-profile fraud case, highlighting her strong character and integrity.
AI generated
NEW YORK - Nancy Kissinger, the wife of former Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger, who shared his whirlwind life of international diplomacy – and then of tarnished celebrity, as a controversial elder statesman – for half a century, died on Aug 20 at her home in South Kent, Connecticut. She was 92.
Her death was announced by her family.
Politically savvy, well versed in global issues and fiercely protective of her husband’s name, Nancy Kissinger travelled widely with him on diplomatic missions after their 1974 marriage. And when Henry Kissinger stepped down three years later, they became a familiar Washington couple at state dinners, embassy parties and Republican White House receptions.
The Kissingers were also among the most visible couples in New York City, their principal residence, attending museum openings, fashion shows by Bill Blass and Oscar de la Renta, and charity fundraisers. Since the early 1980s, their summer and weekend retreat from social obligations had been a 300-acre estate in South Kent.
“To the men and women who know her well,” The New York Times quoted one friend as saying after the wedding, “Mrs Kissinger is an intelligent, capable and warm woman, with a great deal of charm, a good sense of humor and an iron sense of integrity.”
Kissinger’s glamorous life was hardly devoid of trouble, and some of it had to do with her husband’s hotly disputed reputation.
As secretary of state from 1973 to 1977 under Presidents Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford, Henry Kissinger pioneered the policy of detente with the Soviet Union; orchestrated the postwar opening of relations with China; engaged in shuttle diplomacy in the Middle East to end the Arab-Israeli war of 1973, also known as the Yom Kippur War; and helped negotiate the Paris Peace Accords, ending US involvement in the Vietnam War, for which he shared the Nobel Peace Prize.
For all his honours, he remained a polarising figure, accused by journalists and human rights activists of war crimes for supporting the bombing of Hanoi, Vietnam, and an invasion of Cambodia during the Vietnam War; for encouraging a military coup against the socialist government of Salvador Allende in Chile; and for signalling a green light to an Argentine military junta for its “dirty war” against dissidents.
In 1982, walking through a terminal at Newark International Airport in New Jersey, the Kissingers were accosted by Ellen Kaplan, a follower of Lyndon LaRouche, a cult leader with both Marxist and right-wing associations. She shouted insults at both Kissingers, and witnesses said that Nancy Kissinger grabbed the heckler by the throat and threatened to throttle her.
Months later, in a two-hour trial in Newark Municipal Court, Kissinger testified that she had been escorting her husband to Boston for a triple-bypass heart operation and that he was under a doctor’s orders to avoid “upset of any kind”. The judge dismissed a misdemeanor charge of simple assault against Kissinger, saying that there had been no bodily injury.
In the decade before their marriage, his second, Henry Kissinger dated film stars Jill St. John, Liv Ullmann, Shirley MacLaine, Marlo Thomas and others. But his most frequent companion was Nancy Maginnes.
The wedding of Maginnes, 39, and Henry Kissinger, 50, took place in Arlington, Virginia, on March 30, 1974, and while it was attended by only a handful of guests and not disclosed until it was over, it was one of the most heavily covered social events of the year. The Times published the news at the top of Page 1 and followed it with a detailed profile of the bride.
She was a foreign policy specialist for the Commission on Critical Choices for Americans, a creation of former Gov. Nelson Rockefeller of New York. Rockefeller had been the bride’s employer and her husband’s friend and political ally for years, and had introduced them at Harvard, where Henry Kissinger was teaching and Maginnes became one of his students.
Kissinger’s 15-year first marriage to Ann Fleischer had ended in divorce in 1964. They had two children, who both attended the wedding, along with the bride’s brother David and her mother, Agnes Maginnes. Kissinger’s brother, Walter, and his wife were also there, as was Carlyle Maw, a State Department legal adviser.
After the brief civil ceremony, performed by Judge Francis Thomas Jr. of Arlington County Court, the newlyweds flew in Rockefeller’s private jet to Acapulco, Mexico, for a 10-day honeymoon. A dozen Secret Service agents, 20 Mexican police officers and 40 journalists shadowed their every move. Sailing aboard a 30-foot sloop on Acapulco Bay, Henry Kissinger kept a protective arm around his new wife, as a motorboat filled with the press corps followed.
They made a striking couple, not least because the ash-blond, chain-smoking Nancy Kissinger was nearly 6 feet tall, while her husband, recognised around the world, was only 5-foot-8. But friends said they were a good match, intellectually and emotionally, and described them as inseparable.
Two months after the honeymoon, Nancy Kissinger demonstrated her ambassadorial panache by joining her husband’s ongoing shuttle diplomacy in the Middle East, standing for photo ops with Arab and Israeli leaders in various capitals, and attending airborne news briefings in her stockinged feet. Her presence was highlighted in Israeli, Arab and American newspapers.
That autumn, she accompanied her husband to the Soviet Union for his talks with communist leader Leonid Brezhnev on cuts to strategic nuclear arms, and then flew to New Delhi on the second leg of a three-week diplomatic trip to more than a dozen countries. Friends said her poise helped to hide the anxieties that landed her in a hospital with ulcers soon after their return.
In 2009, Nancy Kissinger testified in a criminal court case in New York against Anthony D. Marshall, the son of her friend Brooke Astor, the philanthropist who had died two years before. Marshall had been charged with defrauding his mother’s estate of millions by inducing her to change her will in his favour after her mental capacity had faded. Marshall was convicted and sentenced to a prison term.
Nancy Sharon Maginnes was born in Manhattan on April 13, 1934, the third child and only daughter of Albert B. Maginnes and Agnes (McKinley) Maginnes. Her father, a former pro football player, was a trusts and estates lawyer in White Plains, New York, where Nancy and her two brothers grew up.
The Kissingers had no children. Henry Kissinger died in 2023. Nancy Kissinger’s brother Bristol died in the early 1980s, and her brother David, in 2020. She is survived by two stepchildren, Elizabeth Vandermark and David Kissinger, and five step-grandchildren. NYTIMES
- Ash Wu contributed reporting.
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Jury says The New York Times defamed Alabama basketball player with incorrect story about shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
01:53:02 UTC
10:53:02 KST

Jury says The New York Times defamed Alabama basketball player with incorrect story about shooting
TUSCALOOSA, Ala. (AP) — An Alabama jury on Thursday awarded $9.25 million in damages after finding that The New York Times defamed a college basketball player by incorrectly reporting that he was at the scene of a fatal shooting in Tuscaloosa.
Kai Spears, who played for the University of Alabama men’s team, sued the Times in 2023 after it published a report, citing a person familiar with the investigation, that indicated he was a passenger in a car involved in the shooting. The Times reported that the person had spoken “on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.”
Days later, the Times acknowledged its error in an editor’s note and corrected the story.
The eight-person jury delivered its verdict after a nine-day trial in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Alabama. Matt Glover, an attorney for Spears, said he was pleased with the decision and believes “this verdict will improve journalism throughout the country.”
The Times was reviewing its legal options after losing in court, spokesperson Charlie Stadtlander said.
“We’re disappointed the jury found The Times liable for an honest mistake,” Stadtlander said in a statement Thursday. “We thank the jury for its service, but believe the verdict and award of damages are contrary to law and not supported by the evidence.”
Three other basketball players from the school were present at the January 2023 shooting, which killed a 23-year-old mother. In the lawsuit, Spears claimed the inaccurate reporting had caused him emotional distress and forever linked him with a murder.
A Times article reporting on the verdict Thursday said the newspaper “had not lost a defamation lawsuit brought in the United States over one of its articles in more than 50 years.”

Federal court is asked to block Kennedy Center from returning Trump’s name to building
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21

Federal court is asked to block Kennedy Center from returning Trump’s name to building
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Joyce Beatty made an emergency request on Thursday that a federal court block the Kennedy Center from returning President Donald Trump’s name to the building.
The Trump-aligned board at the Kennedy Center voted earlier this month to inscribe the president’s name on the venue’s facade so it would read “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump.” If the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million, another inscription would be added reading “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.”
The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would also be renamed to recognize Trump.
The Kennedy Center has said it wouldn’t attempt to engrave Trump’s name on the building before Sept. 8 to allow for legal arguments to unfold.
Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex officio member of the Kennedy Center, has led the effort to prevent Trump from memorializing himself there. In asking for the court’s intervention, her lawyers, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, wrote that the board’s actions amounted to “clear violations” of an earlier court order.
A representative for the Kennedy Center didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The resolution approved by Trump’s allies on the board said the Kennedy Center “would be in financial ruin without President Trump’s unique stature as both an unparalleled fundraiser and world-class developer.”
Congress named the performing arts center as a living memorial to Kennedy in 1964, the year after he was assassinated. The law explicitly prohibits the board of trustees from making the center into a memorial to anyone else, and from putting another person’s name on the building’s exterior.
U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump’s name to the building, ordering it removed. The institution’s leaders complied in June but left a tarp and scaffolding in place where Trump’s name once stood.
Lawyers for the Kennedy Center wouldn’t commit this week to taking down the scaffolding, saying it’s needed as part of a broader system for “water testing and structural repairs to the roof overhang.”
